questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Salesforce editions and the AppExchange, per this course.
options: Enterprise is the most common edition for mid-size and larger companies, opening up deeper customization and API access than smaller tiers.
The AppExchange is Salesforce's official marketplace for third-party apps that install directly into an org.
Apps installed from the AppExchange often bring their own custom objects and custom fields into an org.
An edition is purely a price tag — every edition has access to exactly the same features and customization limits.
Essentials is built for very small teams and combines sales and service in one simplified product with the fewest customization options.
Only Unlimited Edition orgs are allowed to install apps from the AppExchange.
questions.explain: Enterprise is indeed the most common tier for mid-size/large companies, and the AppExchange is Salesforce's real marketplace, whose installed apps often bring their own custom objects and fields. Essentials really is the smallest, simplified tier. An edition is not purely price — it sets real feature and customization-limit differences — and the AppExchange is open to any edition, not gated to Unlimited only.

questions.prompt: An analyst wants 'total pipeline value per Account' and builds it by joining Account to Opportunity *through* Contact, instead of joining Account directly to Opportunity. Per this course, what actually happens to the result?
options: Every Opportunity linked to an Account with multiple Contacts gets counted once for each of those Contacts, inflating the total by a factor that depends on Contact count, not the business question.
Salesforce automatically deduplicates the result, so the total pipeline value per Account comes out correct regardless of the join path.
The query fails to run, because Account and Opportunity can't be joined through Contact at all.
The result excludes every Account that has zero Contacts, but is otherwise accurate for every other Account.
questions.explain: This is the double-counting example from Chapter 1: an Opportunity linked to an Account with three Contacts gets counted three times over when the join runs through Contact instead of directly. The query runs successfully and looks plausible, but it's wrong by a factor tied to Contact count — nothing about query syntax catches this, only understanding the actual relationships does.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the ________ is the grid icon in the top-left of every Lightning Experience screen that opens a screen for switching between installed apps.
questions.explain: The App Launcher is the grid icon in the top-left of every Lightning Experience screen. Clicking it opens a full screen listing every installed app, split into 'All Apps' and 'All Items,' with its own search box — the fastest way to jump to an app or object by name.

questions.prompt: Match each core Salesforce vocabulary term to what it actually is, per this course.
right: One piece of data on an object, like Amount or Email
One specific instance of an object, like one particular company's Account
A table-like structure defining a type of thing being tracked, like Account or Contact
questions.explain: An org is one complete, self-contained Salesforce instance. An object is a table-like structure defining a type of thing (Account, Contact). A record is one specific instance of an object — if object is the table, record is the row. A field is one piece of data on an object, like Amount or Email.

questions.prompt: A support manager asks for 'average time to resolve a case' across last quarter. Per this course, is that a Sales Cloud report or a Service Cloud report, and why?
options: Service Cloud, because its center of gravity is the Case object, and resolution time is a Case-lifecycle metric.
Sales Cloud, because resolution time is calculated from the Opportunity object's Close Date field.
It could be either, since Sales Cloud and Service Cloud use entirely separate, unconnected data models.
Sales Cloud, because every support request eventually becomes an Opportunity once it's resolved.
questions.explain: Service Cloud's center of gravity is the Case, tracked from open to resolved — resolution time is a Case-lifecycle metric, not a Sales Cloud one. Sales Cloud and Service Cloud share a platform and foundational objects like Account, but they are not the same data model, and a Case never becomes an Opportunity.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of a prospect's life, per this course's Chapter 2 objects, in the correct order.
items: A raw, unqualified inquiry exists only as a Lead record
The Lead is qualified, and Lead Conversion creates an Account, a Contact, and (usually) an Opportunity
The Opportunity moves through Stage values like Prospecting, Qualification, and Proposal
The Opportunity reaches Closed Won or Closed Lost, ending its run through the pipeline
questions.explain: A deal starts as an unqualified Lead, gets qualified and converted (producing an Account, Contact, and usually an Opportunity), then the resulting Opportunity moves through Stage values until it closes won or lost — the exact order Chapters 2 lays out Leads through Opportunities.

questions.prompt: When a Lead is converted in Salesforce, per this course, what happens to the original Lead record?
options: It's deleted, since its data has been copied to the new Account, Contact, and Opportunity.
It's archived in a separate Leads Archive object that reports can't query directly.
It's marked Converted and stays in the system, now linked to the records it became.
It's converted directly into a Case so support can follow up on it.
It becomes a Campaign Member automatically, tracking which campaign it responded to.
It stays active and unconverted, while a duplicate record is created for the new Account.
questions.explain: Lead Conversion doesn't delete the Lead. The Lead record is marked Converted and stays in the system, now linked to the Account, Contact, and (usually) Opportunity it produced. That link is exactly how an analyst traces a converted Lead's original Lead Source through to the resulting Opportunity's Amount.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A looks plausible because it also assumes the Lead's data moves on to the new records — but it gets the Lead's own fate backwards. The Lead isn't deleted; it's marked Converted and kept, specifically so the analytical trail from Lead Source to Opportunity Amount survives conversion instead of being destroyed.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Opportunity's key fields, per this course.
options: Stage is the field that actually defines the sales pipeline — the pipeline is just open Opportunities grouped by Stage.
Amount is the deal's dollar value, the number summed for 'total pipeline value' or 'revenue closed this quarter.'
Probability is often tied automatically to Stage by default, though it can be overridden on an individual record.
The sales pipeline is a separate Salesforce object from Opportunity, with its own records.
Close Date can only ever hold a deal's actual, already-occurred close date — never an expected future date.
questions.explain: Stage defines the pipeline itself (open Opportunities grouped by Stage), Amount is the dollar value summed for pipeline/revenue totals, and Probability is usually tied to Stage by default but can be overridden. The pipeline is not a separate object — it's just Opportunity data — and Close Date can hold an expected future date as well as an actual one.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the relationship that records what role a specific Contact plays on a specific Opportunity — Decision Maker, Influencer, Economic Buyer — is called a ________.
questions.explain: Contact Roles record not just that a Contact is associated with a deal, but what role they play in it. Answering 'who are the decision makers across our open pipeline' means traversing from Opportunity through Contact Roles to Contact.

questions.prompt: A colleague asks you to 'pull all Activities logged against this Opportunity.' Per this course, which option correctly names the two real Salesforce objects that actually means querying?
options: Task and Event
Lead and Campaign
Case and Contact Role
Account and Contact
questions.explain: 'Activity' is an umbrella term, not a real standalone object — it's really Task (an action item with no fixed calendar time) and Event (something scheduled at a specific time). Salesforce's UI groups them into one 'Activity' related list, which is exactly why the umbrella term persists even though they're two distinct objects underneath.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 2 object to what it represents.
right: The join record connecting a Campaign to a specific Lead or Contact
A person or company that might become a customer, but hasn't been qualified yet
A specific, tracked marketing initiative with its own budget and dates
A real, in-progress or closed deal with a dollar value and close date
questions.explain: A Lead is an unqualified prospect. An Opportunity is a real, in-progress or closed deal with a dollar value and close date. A Campaign is a specific tracked marketing initiative. A Campaign Member is the join record connecting that Campaign to a specific Lead or Contact.

questions.prompt: A support team's total case volume hasn't changed this month, but the count of escalated cases is rising. Per this course, why should an analyst treat that as an early warning sign on its own?
options: A rising escalation count often signals the support team falling behind, even before overall volume looks alarming — it's a leading indicator, not just a side metric.
It isn't actually meaningful, since Escalation Rules are purely cosmetic and don't reflect real case difficulty.
It means the Case Assignment Rules have stopped working entirely and no new cases are being routed.
It means every open Case in the org has automatically been reclassified as Closed Lost.
questions.explain: Escalation Rules fire when a case meets conditions like being open too long relative to its Priority. A rising count of escalations is often an early signal of a team falling behind, well before overall case volume looks alarming on its own — exactly why this lesson calls out escalated cases as their own reporting slice.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Average Handle Time, Case Resolution Time, and First Contact Resolution, per this course.
options: Average Handle Time measures active rep effort on a case, not the total elapsed time a customer experiences.
Case Resolution Time is the total elapsed time from case creation to Closed — the clock a customer actually feels.
First Contact Resolution measures the percentage of cases resolved on the customer's first interaction, with no reopen or escalation.
A team can't have a fast Case Resolution Time while also scoring poorly on First Contact Resolution — the two metrics always move together.
First Contact Resolution is easy to calculate directly from a single standard Salesforce field every org has by default.
questions.explain: AHT measures active rep time, Resolution Time is the customer-felt clock from creation to Closed, and FCR measures first-interaction resolution with no reopen. The two can move independently — a team can resolve cases fast while still prematurely closing and reopening them, hurting FCR — and FCR usually has to be inferred rather than read off one standard field.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the metric measuring the percentage of cases resolved during the customer's very first interaction, with no reopening, escalation, or follow-up, is called ________.
questions.explain: First Contact Resolution (FCR) is the metric that best captures genuine service quality rather than just speed — a team can have a fast average resolution time while still frustrating customers with cases that get closed prematurely and reopened.

questions.prompt: An analyst spots a field called `Renewal_Risk_Score__c` in a report they've never seen before. What does the `__c` suffix actually tell them, per this course?
options: The field is a custom field, built for this org, with a meaning the org's admin defined — not documented anywhere else by default.
The field is a standard Salesforce field that happens to use an unusual naming convention in this org.
The field is a custom field, but its meaning and values are guaranteed to match any other org that has a field with the same name.
The field was created by an AppExchange package and can never be edited by this org's own admin.
The field is a formula field, since only formula fields receive the `__c` suffix.
The field is read-only to every user, since custom fields can't be made editable by Profiles or Permission Sets.
questions.explain: Salesforce marks every custom object and custom field with a `__c` API-name suffix. That suffix means the field was built specifically for this org, and its meaning is whatever that org's admin defined — there's no universal documentation to fall back on, unlike a standard field.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C also correctly calls the field custom, but gets the one detail backwards: custom fields carry no guarantee of consistent meaning across orgs. `Renewal_Risk_Score__c` could be a manually entered picklist in one org and an automatically calculated formula field in another — the `__c` suffix marks a field as org-specific, not as interchangeable between orgs.

questions.prompt: An org has two Opportunity Record Types: 'New Business' (Stage values include Prospecting, Qualification, Proposal) and 'Renewal' (Stage values include Renewal Review, Negotiating, Renewed). A report filters for `Stage = 'Renewal Review'`. What happens to New Business records, and why does this matter?
options: They're excluded entirely, because 'Renewal Review' isn't a Stage value that exists for the New Business Record Type — the report silently misses that whole process.
They're included too, because Stage values are shared identically across every Record Type on the same object.
The report throws an error, because a single filter can't be applied across two different Record Types.
They're automatically converted to the Renewal Record Type so the filter can include them.
questions.explain: Record Types let one object present different picklist values per record. Filtering Stage for a value that only exists on the Renewal Record Type silently excludes every New Business record — not an error, just a quietly incomplete report unless Record Type is checked first.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Salesforce field types, per this course.
options: A Picklist's exact stored values are configured per org, so a filter written for one org's values can silently return nothing in another.
A Lookup field stores a reference to a record on another object.
A Formula field's value is calculated automatically from other fields and can't be edited directly by a user.
Picklist values are fixed by Salesforce itself and are identical across every org that uses that object.
A Currency field stores a plain number with no currency code attached, identical to a Number field.
questions.explain: Picklist values are configured per org — not fixed by Salesforce — which is exactly why a filter from one org can silently fail in another. A Lookup stores a reference to another record; a Formula field is computed automatically and can't be directly edited. A Currency field is stored with a currency code attached, unlike a plain Number field.

questions.prompt: A sales rep insists a field shown in an analyst's Opportunity report 'doesn't exist,' because they've never seen it on their screen. Per this course, what's the most likely explanation, and is the report wrong?
options: The field exists and holds real data, but it simply isn't included on the Page Layout the rep sees — Page Layouts control visibility, not the underlying data, so the report isn't wrong.
The field was deleted from the object after the report was built, so the report is pulling stale, invalid data.
The rep is on a different license tier that blocks the Opportunity object entirely, so the report shouldn't include them at all.
The report is wrong, because any field a user can't see on their own Page Layout cannot legitimately appear in a report.
questions.explain: A Page Layout only controls what a user sees on a page — it has no effect on the underlying data. A field can be populated with real data and simply left off one Page Layout for ordinary reasons, and reports and queries pull directly from the data model, not from any Page Layout.

questions.prompt: Put these checklist questions, per this course, in the order you'd work through them when handed an unfamiliar custom field like `Renewal_Risk_Score__c`.
items: Does its object have Record Types that might change its relevance or valid values?
Is it on the Page Layout you're comparing against?
Who defined it, and why — since there's no universal documentation for a custom field?
questions.explain: This is the four-question checklist from the end of Chapter 4: field type first (Picklist behaves very differently from Formula), then Record Types (relevance or values may differ by type), then Page Layout visibility (a user not recognizing it doesn't mean it's wrong), then the org's own admin or field history as the actual source of truth.

questions.prompt: Why can a roll-up summary field only exist on a Master-Detail relationship, and not on a Lookup relationship, per this course?
options: Master-Detail guarantees every detail record has exactly one master — a relationship that can never be missing — which is the guarantee a roll-up depends on to sum or count reliably.
Lookup relationships are too slow for Salesforce to calculate a roll-up in real time, for performance reasons alone.
Roll-up summary fields are a licensing feature only available to orgs with the Unlimited edition.
Master-Detail relationships store numeric data directly, while Lookup relationships can only store text.
questions.explain: Because Master-Detail guarantees the relationship can't be missing — a detail record cannot be saved without a value in its master field — Salesforce can reliably roll up counts, sums, and min/max values on the master. A Lookup provides no such guarantee, since the child's lookup field can be left blank.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Lookup and Master-Detail relationships, per this course.
options: Deleting a Master-Detail parent automatically cascade-deletes its detail records.
A Master-Detail detail record inherits its security from the master, with no separate sharing setup needed.
A Lookup child record can be saved and exist indefinitely with the lookup field left blank.
Deleting a Lookup parent automatically cascade-deletes every child record pointing at it, by default.
Most relationships in a typical org are Master-Detail, because loose coupling is rarely the right default.
questions.explain: Master-Detail cascade-deletes detail records and inherits security with no extra sharing setup. A Lookup child can be saved with the lookup left blank. Deleting a Lookup parent does not cascade-delete children by default — the lookup is simply cleared — and most relationships in a typical org are actually Lookups, since loose coupling is the right default most of the time.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Salesforce's standard junction object linking Contacts or Leads to Campaigns, carrying its own Status field like 'Sent' or 'Responded,' is called ________.
questions.explain: CampaignMember is Salesforce's standard junction object for the Contacts-to-Campaigns many-to-many problem. Its Status field tracks how one specific Contact engaged with one specific Campaign — data that can only live on the junction record.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 5 concept to its correct description.
right: Salesforce's visual, drag-and-drop tool for viewing an org's object model as connected cards
A custom object with two Master-Detail relationships, implementing many-to-many
A loose, optional link where the child isn't forced to point at a parent
A tight, required link where the child cascade-deletes with its parent
questions.explain: A Lookup relationship is loose and optional. A Master-Detail relationship is tight and required, with cascade delete. A junction object is a custom object with two Master-Detail relationships implementing many-to-many. Schema Builder is Salesforce's visual tool for viewing an org's object model as connected cards.

questions.prompt: Given this course's worked data model, where OpportunityLineItem is a Master-Detail child of Opportunity, why is it safe to assume every OpportunityLineItem has exactly one Opportunity, with no missing or null cases?
options: Because Master-Detail relationships are mandatory — a detail record cannot be saved at all without a value in its master relationship field.
Because Salesforce runs a nightly batch job that deletes any OpportunityLineItem missing an Opportunity reference.
Because OpportunityLineItem is a Lookup child of Opportunity, and Lookups default to a required value in every org.
Because an OpportunityLineItem only exists once an Opportunity has already reached Closed Won.
questions.explain: OpportunityLineItem is a Master-Detail child of Opportunity, and Master-Detail relationships are mandatory — the detail record simply cannot be saved without a master. That guarantee is what lets an analyst roll up line items by Opportunity without worrying about missing or null references.

questions.prompt: Two Sales Reps report to the same Sales Manager in the Role Hierarchy. By default, can one rep see the other rep's records?
options: No — visibility flows upward to the manager above them, but peers at the same level don't automatically see each other's records.
Yes — the Role Hierarchy automatically shares records sideways between anyone reporting to the same manager.
Yes, but only for records created in the last 30 days.
No, and not even their shared manager can see either rep's records without a separate sharing rule.
questions.explain: Visibility flows up the Role Hierarchy, not sideways or downward. The shared manager sees both reps' records because the manager sits above them, but the two reps at the same level don't automatically see each other's records unless a separate sharing rule changes that.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Profiles and Permission Sets, per this course.
options: Every user has exactly one Profile — it's mandatory and not additive with other profiles.
A user can be assigned any number of Permission Sets — zero, one, or several stacked together.
Permission Sets only add permissions on top of a Profile; they never take permissions away.
A Permission Set can override and remove a permission that a user's Profile already grants.
Users are limited to at most one Permission Set in addition to their Profile.
questions.explain: Every user has exactly one mandatory Profile, and can be assigned any number of Permission Sets stacked on top. Permission Sets are additive only — they never remove a permission the Profile already grants, and there's no one-Permission-Set limit.

questions.prompt: A colleague says a report is 'missing data' in one column, but you confirm the underlying field is fully populated for every record. Per this course, what should you check first, and why wouldn't this show up as an error?
options: Field-Level Security on that user's Profile or Permission Set — a hidden field doesn't throw an error, it just doesn't appear or shows blank.
Whether the field was ever added to the object at all, since a report can't reference a field that doesn't exist.
Whether the Role Hierarchy has been deleted for that user, since that would blank every field on every object.
Whether the user's License has expired, since an expired license blanks individual field values but not whole records.
questions.explain: Field-Level Security controls per-field visibility independent of record access, and hiding a field produces no error — it's simply absent from the report builder or shown blank. That silently-missing-value symptom is exactly the practical consequence this lesson flags.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a sharing rule that extends visibility based on field values on the record itself — for example, sharing every Opportunity over $100,000 with the Executive team regardless of owner — is a ________ sharing rule.
questions.explain: A criteria-based sharing rule shares records based on field values on the record itself, regardless of who owns them — distinct from an ownership-based sharing rule, which looks only at who owns the record.

questions.prompt: Put these Chapter 6 access-control layers in the order this course introduces them, from the broadest ceiling on access down to the most fine-grained.
items: License — the hard ceiling on what a user could possibly be granted
Role Hierarchy — which records a user sees by default, based on position
Profile and Permission Sets — what a user can actually do with visible records
Sharing Rules — visibility extended beyond ownership and the Role Hierarchy
Field-Level Security — per-field visibility, independent of record access
questions.explain: Chapter 6 builds these layers in exactly this order: License sets the outer ceiling, Role Hierarchy decides default record visibility, Profiles plus Permission Sets decide what a user can do with what they can see, Sharing Rules extend visibility beyond the hierarchy's defaults, and Field-Level Security operates at the finest, most easily overlooked grain.

questions.prompt: Two users share the exact same job title and the exact same Profile, but one of them can edit a custom object the other user can't touch. Per this course, what's the most likely explanation?
options: The user who can edit it has an additional Permission Set granting that specific access, stacked on top of their shared Profile.
Salesforce randomly varies access between users with identical Profiles to balance system load.
One of the two users must actually have a different License, even though their Profile field shows the same value.
The custom object's Record Type was deleted for one of the two users.
questions.explain: A user's effective access is their Profile's permissions plus every Permission Set assigned to them, unioned together. Two users with an identical Profile can still differ in real access because one of them has an extra Permission Set granting exactly the piece the other lacks — the standard explanation this course gives for this exact scenario.
